17	# LaTeX 论文写作全流程
18	
19	ML/AI 顶会论文从草稿到投稿的完整指南。整合 Orchestra Research、VibeSkills、claim2evidence 三方最佳实践。
20	
21	---
22	
23	## 1. 工作模式
24	
25	开始前选择模式：
26	
27	| 模式 | 说明 | 适用 |
28	|------|------|------|
29	| **Build** | 从实验笔记/结果/代码生成论文 | 新稿 |
30	| **Improve** | 改写已有章节，强化论证 | 修改稿 |
31	| **Audit** | 输出风险列表 + 缺失证据 + 修复建议 | 投前检查 |
32	
33	---
34	
35	## 2. Claim-Evidence 方法论
36	
37	**核心原则：论文是一个有中心贡献的故事，不是实验的堆砌。**
38	
39	### 2.1 一句话贡献
40	
41	在写任何内容之前，必须能用一句话说清贡献。如果不能，说明还没准备好写论文。
42	
43	### 2.2 Claim-Evidence Map
44	
45	为每个 contribution 建立 claim→evidence 映射表：
46	
47	| Contribution | Claim | Evidence | Table/Figure |
48	|-------------|-------|----------|-------------|
49	| C1: 方法 X 在 Y 上 SOTA | 比所有 baseline 高 ≥2% | 5-seed 平均，p<0.05 | Table 1 |
50	| C2: 消融证明 Z 是关键 | 去掉 Z 后掉 >5% | 消融实验 | Table 2 |
51	| C3: 计算效率 | 比 baseline 快 3× | FLOPs + wall-clock | Figure 3 |
52	
53	**没有直接证据支撑的 claim 必须删除或降级为 discussion。**
54	
55	### 2.3 章节起草顺序
56	
57	```
58	1. Introduction + Experiments（先确定 claim 和 evidence）
59	2. Method（评估问题稳定后再写细节）
60	3. Related Work
61	4. Abstract + Title（核心 claim 定型后最后写）
62	```
63	
64	### 2.4 Quality Gates
65	
66	投稿前必须通过：
67	- [ ] 前两段出现显式 novelty 声明
68	- [ ] 每个 contribution 有可验证的 evidence
69	- [ ] Abstract / Intro / Conclusion 的 claim 一致
70	- [ ] Limitations 真实且技术性诚实
71	- [ ] 审稿人两分钟内能识别 delta
72	
73	---
74	
75	## 3. 引用防幻觉（CRITICAL）
76	
77	**AI 生成引用有 ~40% 错误率。绝对禁止凭记忆写 BibTeX。**
78	
79	### 3.1 黄金法则
80	
81	```
82	IF 无法程序化获取引用:
83	    → 标记 [CITATION NEEDED] 或 \cite{PLACEHOLDER_verify}
84	    → 明确告知用户
85	    → 绝不编造看似合理的引用
86	```
87	
88	### 3.2 五步验证流程
89	
90	```
91	1. SEARCH  → Semantic Scholar API 搜索关键词
92	2. VERIFY  → 至少 2 个来源确认论文存在（S2 + arXiv/CrossRef）
93	3. RETRIEVE → 通过 DOI 获取 BibTeX（程序化，非记忆）
94	4. CHECK   → 确认你引用的 claim 确实出自该论文
95	5. ADD     → 加入 .bib 文件
96	```
97	
98	### 3.3 API 速查
99	
100	| API | 用途 | 限制 |
101	|-----|------|------|
102	| **Semantic Scholar** | ML/AI 论文搜索 | 1 RPS (免费) |
103	| **CrossRef** | DOI → BibTeX | 需 mailto 头 |
104	| **arXiv** | 预印本搜索 | 3s 间隔 |
105	
106	```python
107	# DOI → BibTeX（最可靠的方式）
108	import requests
109	def doi_to_bibtex(doi: str) -> str:
110	    r = requests.get(f"https://doi.org/{doi}",
111	                     headers={"Accept": "application/x-bibtex"})
112	    r.raise_for_status()
113	    return r.text
114	
115	# Semantic Scholar 搜索
116	from semanticscholar import SemanticScholar
117	sch = SemanticScholar()
118	results = sch.search_paper("attention mechanism transformers", limit=5)
119	for p in results:
120	    print(f"{p.title} | DOI: {p.externalIds.get('DOI', 'N/A')}")
121	```
122	
123	### 3.4 引用处理规则
124	
125	| 情况 | 处理 |
126	|------|------|
127	| 找到论文 + DOI + BibTeX | 直接用 |
128	| 找到论文，无 DOI | 用 arXiv BibTeX |
129	| 论文存在但无法获取 BibTeX | 标记 placeholder，告知用户 |
130	| 不确定论文是否存在 | 标记 `[CITATION NEEDED]`，告知用户 |
131	| "我觉得有篇关于 X 的论文" | **绝不引用** — 先搜索或标记 |
132	
133	---
134	
135	## 4. 顶会模板速查
136	
137	### 4.1 ML/AI 会议
138	
139	| 会议 | 页数限制 | 主文件 | 样式文件 | 必须项 |
140	|------|---------|--------|---------|--------|
141	| **NeurIPS** | 9 页 | `main.tex` | `neurips.sty` | Paper Checklist |
142	| **ICML** | 8 页 (+1 camera-ready) | `example_paper.tex` | `icml2026.sty` | Broader Impact |
143	| **ICLR** | 9 页 (+1) | `iclr_conference.tex` | `iclr_conference.sty` | LLM 使用声明 |
144	| **ACL/EMNLP** | 8 页 (long) | `acl_latex.tex` | `acl.sty` | Limitations 必须 |
145	| **AAAI** | 7 页 (+1) | `aaai_template.tex` | `aaai.sty` | 严格样式 |
146	| **COLM** | 9 页 (+1) | `colm_conference.tex` | `colm_conference.sty` | 语言模型聚焦 |
147	
148	### 4.2 系统会议
149	
150	| 会议 | 页数限制 | 模板类型 | 关键要求 |
151	|------|---------|---------|---------|
152	| **OSDI** | 12 页 (+2) | USENIX `usenix.sty` | Research / Operational 双 track |
153	| **NSDI** | 12 页 | USENIX | Introduction 预筛 |
154	| **ASPLOS** | 12 页 | ACM `acmart.cls (sigplan)` | 前 2 页快速评审 |
155	| **SOSP** | 12 页 | ACM `acmart.cls (sigplan)` | 可选 Artifact Evaluation |
156	
157	### 4.3 模板使用原则
158	
159	```bash
160	# 1. 复制整个模板目录（不要只拷 .tex）
161	cp -r templates/neurips2025/ ~/papers/my-paper/
162	
163	# 2. 先编译未修改的模板，确认能跑通
164	latexmk -pdf main.tex
165	
166	# 3. 逐章替换内容，频繁编译
167	```
168	
169	**禁止事项：**
170	- 不要修改 `.sty` 文件
171	- 不要在会议模板间复制 `\usepackage` 行
172	- 不要只复制 `.tex` 而不带 `.sty/.bst`
173	
174	---
175	
176	## 5. 写作规范
177	
178	### 5.1 时间分配（Neel Nanda）
179	
180	花**大致相等**的时间在：
181	1. Abstract
182	2. Introduction
183	3. 图表
184	4. **其余所有内容加起来**
185	
186	审稿人读论文的顺序：标题 → 摘要 → 引言 → 图表 → 也许正文。
187	
188	### 5.2 Abstract 五句法（Sebastian Farquhar）
189	
190	```
191	1. 你做了什么（"We introduce/prove/demonstrate..."）
192	2. 为什么这很难且重要
193	3. 怎么做的（含专业关键词以便检索）
194	4. 有什么证据
195	5. 最惊人的数字/结果
196	```
197	
198	删除一切泛泛的开头：~~"Large language models have achieved remarkable success..."~~
199	
200	### 5.3 句子级清晰度（Gopen & Swan）
201	
202	| 原则 | 规则 |
203	|------|------|
204	| 主谓紧邻 | 不要在主语和动词之间插入长从句 |
205	| 重点在句尾 | 把关键数字/结论放在句末 |
206	| 旧信息在前 | 先放读者已知的内容，再引入新概念 |
207	| 动词表达动作 | "We analyzed" 而非 "We performed an analysis" |
208	
209	### 5.4 常见修改
210	
211	| 问题 | 修复 |
212	|------|------|
213	| Abstract 太泛 | 删第一句（如果它能放在任何 ML 论文前面） |
214	| Introduction 超 1.5 页 | 背景挪到 Related Work |
215	| 实验没有显式 claim | 每个实验前加 "This tests whether..." |
216	| 缺统计显著性 | 加 error bars + 运行次数 + 计算方法 |
217	
218	---
219	
220	## 6. 投稿工程链
221	
222	### 6.1 构建
223	
224	```bash
225	# 推荐：latexmk 一键构建
226	latexmk -pdf -interaction=nonstopmode -halt-on-error main.tex
227	
228	# 手动：需要多次编译
229	pdflatex main.tex && bibtex main && pdflatex main.tex && pdflatex main.tex
230	```
231	
232	### 6.2 Lint + 格式化
233	
234	```bash
235	# Lint: 检查常见 LaTeX 问题
236	chktex main.tex
237	
238	# 格式化: 减少 diff 噪声
239	latexindent -w main.tex
240	```
241	
242	### 6.3 图表格式
243	
244	| 类型 | 格式 | 说明 |
245	|------|------|------|
246	| 矢量图（plot、diagram） | PDF | matplotlib: `plt.savefig('fig.pdf')` |
247	| 照片/heatmap | PNG 600dpi 或 TIFF | 栅格图 |
248	| 表格 | `booktabs` 包 | `\toprule/\midrule/\bottomrule` |
249	
250	```latex
251	\usepackage{booktabs}
252	\begin{tabular}{lcc}
253	\toprule
254	Method & Accuracy $\uparrow$ & Latency $\downarrow$ \\
255	\midrule
256	Baseline & 85.2 & 45ms \\
257	\textbf{Ours} & \textbf{92.1} & 38ms \\
258	\bottomrule
259	\end{tabular}
260	```
261	
262	**图表规范：**
263	- 用色盲友好色板（Okabe-Ito 或 Paul Tol）
264	- 图内不放标题（用 caption）
265	- Caption 独立可理解（不依赖正文）
266	- 最佳值加粗，标注方向符号（↑ 越高越好，↓ 越低越好）
267	
268	### 6.4 投稿打包
269	
270	```bash
271	# 清理辅助文件
272	latexmk -c
273	
274	# 打包投稿
275	zip -r submission.zip main.tex *.sty *.bst *.bib figures/ --exclude='*.aux' --exclude='*.log'
276	```
277	
278	### 6.5 常见失败点
279	
280	| 问题 | 解决 |
281	|------|------|
282	| 图片格式混用导致编译失败 | 统一用 PDF |
283	| 字体未嵌入 | `pdffonts output.pdf` 检查 |
284	| Overfull box 过多 | 关键位置手动调行 |
285	| 引用缺字段 | 检查 DOI/年份/期刊名 |
286	| 超页数 | 用 `\vspace{-Xpt}` 微调，或精简内容 |
287	
288	---
289	
290	## 7. 会议转投
291	
292	当论文被拒或转投其他会议时：
293	
294	### 7.1 ML/AI 会议间转换
295	
296	| 转换 | 页数变化 | 关键调整 |
297	|------|---------|---------|
298	| NeurIPS → ICML | 9→8 | 删 1 页，加 Broader Impact |
299	| ICML → ICLR | 8→9 | 可扩展实验 + LLM 声明 |
300	| NeurIPS → ACL | 9→8 | 按 NLP 惯例重组 + Limitations |
301	| ICLR → AAAI | 9→7 | 大幅精简，严格样式 |
302	
303	### 7.2 转投原则
304	
305	1. **永远用目标模板重新开始** — 复制目标模板，迁移内容，不要合并 preamble
306	2. **只迁移正文内容** — 不复制 `\usepackage`、header/footer 命令
307	3. **根据审稿意见改进** — 但不要在新稿中提及旧投稿（双盲）
308	4. **检查目标会议特殊要求** — checklist、ethics statement、LLM 声明等
309	
310	---
311	
312	## 8. 投前清单
313	
314	### 通用清单
315	
316	- [ ] Abstract/Intro/Conclusion 的 claim 一致
317	- [ ] 每个 contribution 有对应 evidence
318	- [ ] 所有引用已程序化验证（无幻觉引用）
319	- [ ] Error bars + 运行次数 + 统计方法
320	- [ ] Limitations 章节存在且诚实
321	- [ ] 匿名化（双盲审稿）
322	- [ ] 符合页数限制
323	- [ ] 所有图表有自包含 caption
324	- [ ] `.bib` 中无缺失字段
325	- [ ] PDF 编译无 warning
326	
327	### 会议特定
328	
329	| 会议 | 额外要求 |
330	|------|---------|
331	| NeurIPS | 16 项 Paper Checklist（附录，不计页数） |
332	| ICML | Broader Impact Statement |
333	| ICLR | LLM 使用声明 |
334	| ACL/EMNLP | Limitations 章节（必须），Ethics Statement |
335	| AAAI | 严格样式文件合规 |
336	
337	---
338	
339	## 参考资源
340	
341	**写作方法论：**
342	- [Neel Nanda: How to Write ML Papers](https://www.alignmentforum.org/posts/eJGptPbbFPZGLpjsp/) — What/Why/So What 框架
343	- [Farquhar: How to Write ML Papers](https://sebastianfarquhar.com/on-research/2024/11/04/how_to_write_ml_papers/) — 五句法 Abstract
344	- [Gopen & Swan: Science of Scientific Writing](https://cseweb.ucsd.edu/~swanson/papers/science-of-writing.pdf) — 读者预期 7 原则
345	- [Lipton: Heuristics for Scientific Writing](https://www.approximatelycorrect.com/2018/01/29/heuristics-technical-scientific-writing-machine-learning-perspective/) — 用词
346	- [Perez: Easy Paper Writing Tips](https://ethanperez.net/easy-paper-writing-tips/) — 微观清晰度
347	
348	**API：**
349	- [Semantic Scholar](https://api.semanticscholar.org/api-docs/) | [CrossRef](https://www.crossref.org/documentation/) | [arXiv](https://info.arxiv.org/help/api/)
350	
351	**会议官方：**
352	- [NeurIPS](https://neurips.cc/) | [ICML](https://icml.cc/) | [ICLR](https://iclr.cc/) | [ACL](https://www.aclweb.org/) | [AAAI](https://aaai.org/) | [EMNLP](https://2025.emnlp.org/)

# LaTeX 论文写作全流程

ML/AI 顶会论文从草稿到投稿的完整指南。整合 Orchestra Research、VibeSkills、claim2evidence 三方最佳实践。

---

## 1. 工作模式

开始前选择模式：

| 模式 | 说明 | 适用 |
|------|------|------|
| **Build** | 从实验笔记/结果/代码生成论文 | 新稿 |
| **Improve** | 改写已有章节，强化论证 | 修改稿 |
| **Audit** | 输出风险列表 + 缺失证据 + 修复建议 | 投前检查 |

---

## 2. Claim-Evidence 方法论

**核心原则：论文是一个有中心贡献的故事，不是实验的堆砌。**

### 2.1 一句话贡献

在写任何内容之前，必须能用一句话说清贡献。如果不能，说明还没准备好写论文。

### 2.2 Claim-Evidence Map

为每个 contribution 建立 claim→evidence 映射表：

| Contribution | Claim | Evidence | Table/Figure |
|-------------|-------|----------|-------------|
| C1: 方法 X 在 Y 上 SOTA | 比所有 baseline 高 ≥2% | 5-seed 平均，p<0.05 | Table 1 |
| C2: 消融证明 Z 是关键 | 去掉 Z 后掉 >5% | 消融实验 | Table 2 |
| C3: 计算效率 | 比 baseline 快 3× | FLOPs + wall-clock | Figure 3 |

**没有直接证据支撑的 claim 必须删除或降级为 discussion。**

### 2.3 章节起草顺序

```
1. Introduction + Experiments（先确定 claim 和 evidence）
2. Method（评估问题稳定后再写细节）
3. Related Work
4. Abstract + Title（核心 claim 定型后最后写）
```

### 2.4 Quality Gates

投稿前必须通过：
- [ ] 前两段出现显式 novelty 声明
- [ ] 每个 contribution 有可验证的 evidence
- [ ] Abstract / Intro / Conclusion 的 claim 一致
- [ ] Limitations 真实且技术性诚实
- [ ] 审稿人两分钟内能识别 delta

---

## 3. 引用防幻觉（CRITICAL）

**AI 生成引用有 ~40% 错误率。绝对禁止凭记忆写 BibTeX。**

### 3.1 黄金法则

```
IF 无法程序化获取引用:
    → 标记 [CITATION NEEDED] 或 \cite{PLACEHOLDER_verify}
    → 明确告知用户
    → 绝不编造看似合理的引用
```

### 3.2 五步验证流程

```
1. SEARCH  → Semantic Scholar API 搜索关键词
2. VERIFY  → 至少 2 个来源确认论文存在（S2 + arXiv/CrossRef）
3. RETRIEVE → 通过 DOI 获取 BibTeX（程序化，非记忆）
4. CHECK   → 确认你引用的 claim 确实出自该论文
5. ADD     → 加入 .bib 文件
```

### 3.3 API 速查

| API | 用途 | 限制 |
|-----|------|------|
| **Semantic Scholar** | ML/AI 论文搜索 | 1 RPS (免费) |
| **CrossRef** | DOI → BibTeX | 需 mailto 头 |
| **arXiv** | 预印本搜索 | 3s 间隔 |

```python
# DOI → BibTeX（最可靠的方式）
import requests
def doi_to_bibtex(doi: str) -> str:
    r = requests.get(f"https://doi.org/{doi}",
                     headers={"Accept": "application/x-bibtex"})
    r.raise_for_status()
    return r.text

# Semantic Scholar 搜索
from semanticscholar import SemanticScholar
sch = SemanticScholar()
results = sch.search_paper("attention mechanism transformers", limit=5)
for p in results:
    print(f"{p.title} | DOI: {p.externalIds.get('DOI', 'N/A')}")
```

### 3.4 引用处理规则

| 情况 | 处理 |
|------|------|
| 找到论文 + DOI + BibTeX | 直接用 |
| 找到论文，无 DOI | 用 arXiv BibTeX |
| 论文存在但无法获取 BibTeX | 标记 placeholder，告知用户 |
| 不确定论文是否存在 | 标记 `[CITATION NEEDED]`，告知用户 |
| "我觉得有篇关于 X 的论文" | **绝不引用** — 先搜索或标记 |

---

## 4. 顶会模板速查

### 4.1 ML/AI 会议

| 会议 | 页数限制 | 主文件 | 样式文件 | 必须项 |
|------|---------|--------|---------|--------|
| **NeurIPS** | 9 页 | `main.tex` | `neurips.sty` | Paper Checklist |
| **ICML** | 8 页 (+1 camera-ready) | `example_paper.tex` | `icml2026.sty` | Broader Impact |
| **ICLR** | 9 页 (+1) | `iclr_conference.tex` | `iclr_conference.sty` | LLM 使用声明 |
| **ACL/EMNLP** | 8 页 (long) | `acl_latex.tex` | `acl.sty` | Limitations 必须 |
| **AAAI** | 7 页 (+1) | `aaai_template.tex` | `aaai.sty` | 严格样式 |
| **COLM** | 9 页 (+1) | `colm_conference.tex` | `colm_conference.sty` | 语言模型聚焦 |

### 4.2 系统会议

| 会议 | 页数限制 | 模板类型 | 关键要求 |
|------|---------|---------|---------|
| **OSDI** | 12 页 (+2) | USENIX `usenix.sty` | Research / Operational 双 track |
| **NSDI** | 12 页 | USENIX | Introduction 预筛 |
| **ASPLOS** | 12 页 | ACM `acmart.cls (sigplan)` | 前 2 页快速评审 |
| **SOSP** | 12 页 | ACM `acmart.cls (sigplan)` | 可选 Artifact Evaluation |

### 4.3 模板使用原则

```bash
# 1. 复制整个模板目录（不要只拷 .tex）
cp -r templates/neurips2025/ ~/papers/my-paper/

# 2. 先编译未修改的模板，确认能跑通
latexmk -pdf main.tex

# 3. 逐章替换内容，频繁编译
```

**禁止事项：**
- 不要修改 `.sty` 文件
- 不要在会议模板间复制 `\usepackage` 行
- 不要只复制 `.tex` 而不带 `.sty/.bst`

---

## 5. 写作规范

### 5.1 时间分配（Neel Nanda）

花**大致相等**的时间在：
1. Abstract
2. Introduction
3. 图表
4. **其余所有内容加起来**

审稿人读论文的顺序：标题 → 摘要 → 引言 → 图表 → 也许正文。

### 5.2 Abstract 五句法（Sebastian Farquhar）

```
1. 你做了什么（"We introduce/prove/demonstrate..."）
2. 为什么这很难且重要
3. 怎么做的（含专业关键词以便检索）
4. 有什么证据
5. 最惊人的数字/结果
```

删除一切泛泛的开头：~~"Large language models have achieved remarkable success..."~~

### 5.3 句子级清晰度（Gopen & Swan）

| 原则 | 规则 |
|------|------|
| 主谓紧邻 | 不要在主语和动词之间插入长从句 |
| 重点在句尾 | 把关键数字/结论放在句末 |
| 旧信息在前 | 先放读者已知的内容，再引入新概念 |
| 动词表达动作 | "We analyzed" 而非 "We performed an analysis" |

| 问题 | 修复 |
|------|------|
| Abstract 太泛 | 删第一句（如果它能放在任何 ML 论文前面） |
| Introduction 超 1.5 页 | 背景挪到 Related Work |
| 实验没有显式 claim | 每个实验前加 "This tests whether..." |
| 缺统计显著性 | 加 error bars + 运行次数 + 计算方法 |

```bash

latexmk -pdf -interaction=nonstopmode -halt-on-error main.tex

```

Method & Accuracy $\uparrow$ & Latency $\downarrow$ \\
\midrule

% Introduction: Structural stagnation detection in LLM coding agents (EMNLP 2026 ARR)
\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:introduction}

Large language model (LLM) agents are increasingly deployed for complex, long-horizon software engineering tasks---resolving GitHub issues, debugging production systems, and iterating on code across multiple rounds of edits \citep{jimenez2024swebench,yang2024sweagent,wang2025openhands}.
As task complexity grows, a critical failure mode emerges that is qualitatively different from crashes or syntax errors: the agent \emph{stagnates}---continuing to produce actions that appear diverse on the surface while making no meaningful progress toward the task goal.
\citet{orlanski2026slopcodebench} systematically document this degradation in long-horizon coding tasks, finding structural erosion in 77\% of agent trajectories and verbosity increases in 75.5\%, with no agent fully solving any benchmark problem end-to-end.
Unlike overt loops, stagnation is insidious: the agent issues varied commands, edits different files, and generates plausible-looking outputs, yet its behavior is functionally stuck.
Detecting when an agent has entered this regime is essential for reliable deployment---enabling interventions such as early termination, strategy switching, or human escalation---yet identifying \emph{what signals} carry stagnation information, and whether complex language understanding is necessary to extract them, remains an open question.

Prior approaches to monitoring agent behavior address aspects of this problem but none systematically investigate what information is needed for detection.
\emph{Repetition detectors} identify exact or near-exact loops in action sequences, catching the simplest failure mode but missing semantically diverse stagnation where the agent varies its surface behavior while remaining functionally stuck.
\emph{Process reward models} \citep{xi2025agentprm} assign quality scores to individual actions, enabling search-time guidance, but step-level granularity cannot capture temporal patterns that distinguish transient setbacks from sustained stagnation---a distinction that requires reasoning over windows of consecutive actions \citep{chen2025monitoring}.
\emph{Self-reflection} frameworks \citep{shinn2023reflexion,yao2023tot,zhou2024lats} rely on the agent itself to diagnose and recover from failures, but when the agent is genuinely stuck, self-diagnosis amounts to querying the failing model about its own failure---a circularity that limits reliability.
More fundamentally, all three lines of work prescribe detection \emph{methods} without first asking what kinds of signals actually carry stagnation information: does detecting subtle agent failure require sophisticated semantic understanding, or do simpler structural patterns suffice?

We present an empirical analysis that addresses this gap.
Using a weak supervision framework \citep{ratner2016dataprogramming,ratner2017snorkel}, we construct silver-labeled datasets from trajectories of two architecturally distinct agents: SWE-Agent \citep{yang2024sweagent} on SWE-bench \citep{jimenez2024swebench} (54,809 windows) and OpenHands \citep{wang2025openhands} (150,652 windows).
Three labeling functions (LFs)---targeting command repetition, file modification patterns, and task outcome---provide noisy votes that are aggregated via majority vote into window-level binary labels.
Against these silver labels, we systematically compare three detection paradigms: hand-crafted structural features, neural embedding probes, and LLM-as-judge evaluation.

Our central finding is that \textbf{stagnation signals are fundamentally structural, not semantic}.
Thirty hand-crafted features capturing command repetition rates, file operation counts, and edit distances achieve 0.9951 macro-F1 in-domain and 0.967 on zero-shot cross-agent transfer, exceeding the LLM judge by 33.3 percentage points (pp).
A GRU-based neural probe \citep{cho2014gru} over sentence embeddings reaches 0.906 in-domain but collapses to 0.528 on zero-shot transfer and recovers only to 0.751 after full fine-tuning on the target agent.
The structural advantage is encoder-agnostic: swapping the probe's embedding backbone across three encoders (Qwen3-0.6B, BGE-M3, E5-large-v2) yields probe F1 consistently above 0.90 \citep{zhang2025qwen3embedding,chen2024bgem3,wang2024e5}, confirming that the temporal architecture rather than a specific pretrained encoder drives embedding-based performance.
Critically, the gap between structural features and learned representations persists across agents with substantially different action distributions (28.5\% vs.\ 6.6\% stagnation rates), suggesting that stagnation manifests in action-level structure that generalizes without adaptation.
This challenges the prevailing intuition that detecting subtle agent failures requires complex language understanding, and suggests that lightweight structural monitoring---requiring no GPU and running in under 5\,ms per window---may be more practical than neural or LLM-based approaches for real-time agent oversight.

Beyond static detection, we analyze the temporal dynamics of the labeling functions that generate silver labels.
On SWE-Agent, command repetition ($\lambda_1$) leads stagnation onset by 1.87 steps on average, serving as an early warning signal, while outcome backpropagation ($\lambda_3$) lags by 6.70 steps (Kruskal-Wallis $H{=}274.3$, $p{<}10^{-59}$).
However, this temporal structure is agent-specific: on OpenHands, $\lambda_1$ reverses from leading to lagging ($+3.32$ steps), firing on 92.3\% of windows with a 71\% false positive rate on progress windows.
Removing $\lambda_1$ from the OpenHands labeling pipeline improves fine-tuned probe F1 by 17.6\,pp, demonstrating that labeling functions validated on one agent architecture can become adversarial on another.
This finding establishes that LF temporal roles must be re-validated per agent and motivates the circular evaluation methodology we develop to surface such pathologies (\S\ref{sec:cmd_rep_ablation}).

We further investigate whether encoding this temporal structure into label aggregation can improve over simple majority vote.
Three temporal label models---time-varying weights (TWV), Hidden Markov Models \citep{safranchik2020linkedhmm}, and lag-aware HMMs---all fail to surpass majority vote on downstream stagnation detection.
TWV achieves marginally higher self-evaluated F1 (+0.57\,pp) but degrades downstream probe performance by 2.57\,pp; the standard HMM overpredicts stagnation, dropping downstream F1 to 0.656.
This negative result demonstrates that temporal sophistication in label aggregation does not translate to better silver labels when base agreement among LFs is already high.

Our contributions are:
\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=*,itemsep=2pt]
    \item \textbf{Structural signal discovery.} We show that 30 structural features achieve near-perfect stagnation detection (0.9951 in-domain, 0.967 cross-agent macro-F1), outperforming neural probes and LLM judges by wide margins (+33.3\,pp over LLM-as-judge). To our knowledge, this is the first systematic comparison demonstrating that stagnation information resides in action-level structure rather than semantic content.
    \item \textbf{Labeling function temporal dynamics.} We reveal that LFs occupy statistically distinct temporal niches relative to stagnation onset, with agent-specific reversals that corrupt silver labels. We develop a circular evaluation methodology to identify and quantify these cross-agent pathologies.
    \item \textbf{Temporal label model negative finding.} We show that three temporal label models fail to improve over majority vote for downstream detection, despite clear temporal structure in LF firing patterns. This informs future weak supervision design for sequential agent data.
\end{enumerate}

3	
4	We evaluate stagnation detection across four axes: in-domain accuracy, cross-agent transfer, robustness to design choices, and temporal dynamics of labeling functions.
5	All reported metrics are evaluated against silver labels derived from majority vote over three labeling functions (\S\ref{sec:method}).

7	\paragraph{Circular evaluation caveat.}
8	Structural features (command repetition ratios, file operation counts, edit distances) are computed from the same signals that the labeling functions use to produce silver labels.

18	\label{sec:why_tlm_fail}
19	
20	Despite clear temporal structure in LF activations (\S\ref{sec:lf_temporal}), no temporal label model improves downstream detection over majority vote (\S\ref{sec:temporal_label_models}).

22	
23	TWV targets only conf${=}1$ windows, flipping 14.1\% of their labels.
24	These flips introduce noise rather than corrections---downstream probe F1 drops by 2.57\,pp relative to MV-trained.

26	Lag-HMM, despite explicitly modeling per-LF temporal offsets, tracks MV within 0.1\,pp---the offset information captured by individual LFs (\S\ref{sec:lf_temporal}) does not translate into better aggregation.
27	
28	Three binary LFs produce at most $2^3{=}8$ voting patterns, yielding too little conflict for temporal models to exploit.

48	\label{sec:ob_analysis}

\section{Analysis}
\label{sec:analysis}

\subsection{Circular Evaluation and Its Implications}
\label{sec:circular}

The structural RF's 0.9951 macro-F1 (\S\ref{sec:main_results}) is a predictable consequence of feature--label overlap, not a detection achievement.
The 30 structural features include repetition ratios and file operation counts---the same signals $\lambda_1$ and $\lambda_2$ consume to produce silver labels.
This score therefore represents an upper bound on LF reverse-engineering fidelity.

Two evaluation settings break this circularity.
First, cross-agent transfer: GB trained on SWE-Agent LF distributions achieves 0.9674 macro-F1 on OpenHands, where LF firing patterns differ substantially (e.g., cmd\_rep fires on 92.3\% vs.\ 65.6\% of windows).
The model cannot memorize LF outputs when tested on a different agent's distribution.
Second, a human-annotated gold set (\S\ref{sec:gold_set}) will provide definitive non-circular ground truth.
Until then, all in-domain structural metrics should be interpreted as LF-agreement scores rather than detection accuracy.

\subsection{Why Temporal Label Models Fail}
\label{sec:why_tlm_fail}

Despite clear temporal structure in LF activations (\S\ref{sec:lf_temporal}), no temporal label model improves downstream detection over majority vote (\S\ref{sec:temporal_label_models}).
The root cause is low label conflict in the 3-LF regime: conf${\geq}$2 windows dominate the training set, leaving few ambiguous labels for temporal models to correct.

TWV targets only conf${=}1$ windows, flipping 14.1\% of their labels.
These flips introduce noise rather than corrections---downstream probe F1 drops by 2.57\,pp relative to MV-trained.
HMM overpredicts stagnation (29,176 vs.\ 25,633 progress windows), producing a distorted label distribution that degrades the probe to 0.6564.
Lag-HMM, despite explicitly modeling per-LF temporal offsets, tracks MV within 0.1\,pp---the offset information captured by individual LFs (\S\ref{sec:lf_temporal}) does not translate into better aggregation.

Three binary LFs produce at most $2^3{=}8$ voting patterns, yielding too little conflict for temporal models to exploit.
A richer LF set ($>$10 functions with higher disagreement rates) would be needed to create the ambiguity where temporal aggregation could add value \citep{ratner2017snorkel}.

\subsection{Error Analysis}
\label{sec:error_analysis}

We analyze errors of the ProgressProbe (GRU) on the SWE-Agent conf${\geq}$2 test set under the stagnation-positive convention (positive = stagnation throughout).
The model misclassifies 131 of 1,824 windows (7.2\% error rate): 85 false negatives (predicted progress, actual stagnation; 64.9\% of errors) and 46 false positives (predicted stagnation, actual progress; 35.1\%).

The recall bottleneck is the dominant failure mode: $P_\text{stag}{=}0.897$ vs.\ $R_\text{stag}{=}0.825$.
Missed stagnation windows (FN) are not borderline cases---the model assigns them a mean stagnation probability of only 0.078 (i.e., high progress confidence of 0.922), with 73\% receiving $>$0.9 progress probability.
These windows feature agents performing diverse edits and varied commands that mimic progress patterns while making no effective headway, constituting a systematic blind spot.
False positives arise when agents repeat specific command patterns during genuine progress.

LF conflict is a strong error predictor: 39.7\% of error windows have at least one LF disagreeing, compared to a 31\% base rate.
The cmd\_rep LF contributes the highest per-LF error rate (12.75\%).
Errors concentrate in trajectory midpoints (10.2\% error rate vs.\ 6.5\% at endpoints), where the boundary between exploration and stagnation is most ambiguous.
Error mass is also non-uniform across trajectories: the two highest-error trajectories account for 18.3\% of all misclassifications.

\subsection{Outcome Backpropagation as Distant Supervision}
\label{sec:ob_analysis}

Outcome backpropagation ($\lambda_3$) is a privileged signal that uses task outcome, unavailable at inference time.
A 3-seed split-isolated holdout removing $\lambda_3$ yields macro-F1 of $0.770{\pm}0.022$, a 7.7\,pp drop from the 3-LF baseline of 0.847.
$\lambda_3$ contributes 33.5\% of conf${\geq}$2 labels (5,158 of 15,401 windows).

However, $\lambda_3$ functions as a coverage expander rather than an independent corrector: across 43,402 windows where both 2-LF and 3-LF configurations produce labels, their agreement is 100\%.
$\lambda_3$ never flips a majority vote---it only promotes conf${=}1$ windows to conf${=}2$ by adding a third agreeing vote.
This suggests that additional real-time LFs targeting the same coverage gaps could replace the privileged outcome signal without sacrificing label quality.

1	% Related Work: Structural stagnation detection in LLM coding agents (EMNLP 2026 ARR)
2	\section{Related Work}
3	\label{sec:related_work}
4	
5	\subsection{LLM Agent Monitoring and Evaluation}
6	
7	As LLM agents tackle increasingly complex tasks \citep{jimenez2024swebench,yang2024sweagent,wang2025openhands,zhou2024webarena,wang2024mint}, understanding and monitoring their failure modes has become critical.
8	Taxonomic studies reveal that agent failures are often systematic: \citet{cemri2025multiagentfail} identify 14 failure modes in multi-agent systems, including step repetition as a concrete symptom, while \citet{zhu2025agentfail} show that cascading failures---where a single root cause propagates across subsequent decisions---dominate long-horizon tasks.
9	\citet{orlanski2026slopcodebench} provide the most direct evidence of agent degradation, documenting structural erosion in 77\% of coding agent trajectories with no agent fully solving any benchmark task end-to-end.
10	
11	Existing monitoring approaches span several paradigms.
12	\emph{Self-reflection} methods \citep{shinn2023reflexion,yao2023tot,zhou2024lats} rely on the agent to diagnose its own failures, but \citet{huang2024selfcorrect} and \citet{kamoi2024selfcorrection} demonstrate that LLMs cannot reliably self-correct without external feedback, motivating external monitoring.
13	\citet{george2025cycledetection} propose unsupervised cycle detection combining call-stack analysis with embedding similarity, while \citet{pipis2025reasoningloop} analyze why reasoning models loop, using $n$-gram repetition as a detection heuristic.
14	On the external monitoring front, \citet{chen2025monitoring} show that sequence-level context is necessary---single-step analysis misses sequentially contextual harm---and \citet{kale2025weaktostrong} demonstrate that monitor scaffolding matters more than monitor capability, with weak models reliably monitoring stronger agents.
15	
16	Our work differs from all of the above in its central question: rather than proposing a new monitoring \emph{method}, we conduct an empirical study asking what \emph{signals} carry stagnation information.
17	We show that 30 structural features suffice for near-perfect detection (0.995 F1), without requiring another LLM, self-reflection, or embedding-based similarity.
18	
19	\subsection{Process Reward Models for Agents}
20	
21	Process reward models (PRMs) assign quality scores to individual agent steps, enabling search-time guidance and trajectory selection.
22	\citet{xi2025agentprm} introduce AgentPRM, training step-level reward models via TD/GAE that evaluate both ``promise'' (long-term potential) and ``progress'' (immediate advancement), achieving 8$\times$ compute efficiency gains.
23	\citet{choudhury2025prm} formalize the PRM framework and propose InversePRM, learning process rewards from expert demonstrations without outcome labels, with a 3B model surpassing GPT-4o.
24	Evaluation benchmarks have emerged in parallel: \citet{li2026toolprmbench} benchmark PRMs on tool-use scenarios, finding that specialized PRMs substantially outperform general-purpose ones, while \citet{wang2026planrewardbench} evaluate trajectory-level reward models and reveal that all model categories---generative, discriminative, and LLM-as-judge---degrade significantly on long-horizon trajectories.
25	\citet{fan2026agentrm} extend PRMs with structured reasoning traces and multi-dimensional critiques (Agent-RRM), and \citet{qiu2026dataprm} address data analysis agents specifically, introducing environment-aware probing to detect silent errors that standard PRMs miss.

\section{Related Work}
\label{sec:related_work}

\subsection{LLM Agent Monitoring and Evaluation}

As LLM agents tackle increasingly complex tasks \citep{jimenez2024swebench,yang2024sweagent,wang2025openhands,zhou2024webarena,wang2024mint}, understanding and monitoring their failure modes has become critical.
Taxonomic studies reveal that agent failures are often systematic: \citet{cemri2025multiagentfail} identify 14 failure modes in multi-agent systems, including step repetition as a concrete symptom, while \citet{zhu2025agentfail} show that cascading failures---where a single root cause propagates across subsequent decisions---dominate long-horizon tasks.
\citet{orlanski2026slopcodebench} provide the most direct evidence of agent degradation, documenting structural erosion in 77\% of coding agent trajectories with no agent fully solving any benchmark task end-to-end.

Existing monitoring approaches span several paradigms.
\emph{Self-reflection} methods \citep{shinn2023reflexion,yao2023tot,zhou2024lats} rely on the agent to diagnose its own failures, but \citet{huang2024selfcorrect} and \citet{kamoi2024selfcorrection} demonstrate that LLMs cannot reliably self-correct without external feedback, motivating external monitoring.
\citet{george2025cycledetection} propose unsupervised cycle detection combining call-stack analysis with embedding similarity, while \citet{pipis2025reasoningloop} analyze why reasoning models loop, using $n$-gram repetition as a detection heuristic.
On the external monitoring front, \citet{chen2025monitoring} show that sequence-level context is necessary---single-step analysis misses sequentially contextual harm---and \citet{kale2025weaktostrong} demonstrate that monitor scaffolding matters more than monitor capability, with weak models reliably monitoring stronger agents.

Our work differs from all of the above in its central question: rather than proposing a new monitoring \emph{method}, we conduct an empirical study asking what \emph{signals} carry stagnation information.
We show that 30 structural features suffice for near-perfect detection (0.995 F1), without requiring another LLM, self-reflection, or embedding-based similarity.

\subsection{Process Reward Models for Agents}

Process reward models (PRMs) assign quality scores to individual agent steps, enabling search-time guidance and trajectory selection.
\citet{xi2025agentprm} introduce AgentPRM, training step-level reward models via TD/GAE that evaluate both ``promise'' (long-term potential) and ``progress'' (immediate advancement), achieving 8$\times$ compute efficiency gains.
\citet{choudhury2025prm} formalize the PRM framework and propose InversePRM, learning process rewards from expert demonstrations without outcome labels, with a 3B model surpassing GPT-4o.
Evaluation benchmarks have emerged in parallel: \citet{li2026toolprmbench} benchmark PRMs on tool-use scenarios, finding that specialized PRMs substantially outperform general-purpose ones, while \citet{wang2026planrewardbench} evaluate trajectory-level reward models and reveal that all model categories---generative, discriminative, and LLM-as-judge---degrade significantly on long-horizon trajectories.
\citet{fan2026agentrm} extend PRMs with structured reasoning traces and multi-dimensional critiques (Agent-RRM), and \citet{qiu2026dataprm} address data analysis agents specifically, introducing environment-aware probing to detect silent errors that standard PRMs miss.

Our work is complementary to the PRM line but differs in three fundamental ways: (1)~we operate at window level rather than step level, capturing temporal patterns across consecutive actions; (2)~we require no outcome labels or reward annotations---our labeling functions use only observable structural signals; and (3)~our goal is real-time \emph{monitoring} (stagnation detection in $<$5\,ms), not \emph{training signal} generation for agent improvement.
The degradation of trajectory-level reward models on long horizons reported by \citet{wang2026planrewardbench} further motivates our window-level approach, which avoids full-trajectory reasoning by design.

\subsection{Data Programming and Weak Supervision}

Data programming \citep{ratner2016dataprogramming} enables rapid training set creation through user-defined labeling functions (LFs), with a generative model learning LF accuracies to produce probabilistic labels.
Snorkel \citep{ratner2017snorkel} operationalizes this into an end-to-end system with dependency-aware label models, and \citet{fu2020flyingsquid} accelerate label model inference via closed-form triplet methods.
\citet{zhang2021wrench} provide a comprehensive benchmark spanning 22 datasets, though all assume i.i.d.\ data points.

Extensions to sequential data relax this assumption.
\citet{safranchik2020linkedhmm} introduce a linked HMM for weakly supervised sequence tagging (NER), incorporating linking rules that model span structure and improving over i.i.d.\ label models by 7~F1 points.
\citet{sala2019multiresolution} handle multi-resolution LFs operating at different temporal granularities.
In crowdsourcing, \citet{nguyen2017hmmcrowd} extend \citeauthor{dawid1979em}'s EM-based annotator model \citep{dawid1979em} with HMM structure for sequential label aggregation.

We apply data programming to agent trajectory data, a novel domain where LFs exhibit systematic temporal dynamics (e.g., command repetition leads stagnation onset by 1.87 steps on SWE-Agent).
Unlike prior sequential extensions that target token-level NER or multi-resolution alignment, our setting involves window-level binary classification with agent-specific LF role reversals.
Critically, we test whether temporal label models---motivated by the clear i.i.d.\ violations we observe---can improve over majority vote, and report a negative finding: three implementations (TWV, HMM, lag-aware HMM) all fail to surpass simple voting in the low-conflict regime of our 3-LF framework.

\subsection{Anomaly Detection in Agent Trajectories}

Detecting anomalous behavior in sequential agent data connects to the broader literature on time-series anomaly detection.
\citet{liu2026trajad} propose TrajAD, training a fine-grained verifier through synthetic perturbations (perturb-and-complete) to detect trajectory anomalies including task failure, process inefficiency, and unwarranted continuation.
They show that general-purpose LLMs perform poorly at zero-shot trajectory anomaly detection, motivating specialized approaches.

Our work differs from anomaly detection in both formulation and methodology.
We frame stagnation as a binary classification problem over sliding windows rather than identifying rare deviations from a normal distribution.
Stagnation is not anomalous in the statistical sense---it occurs in 28.5\% of SWE-Agent windows and 6.6\% of OpenHands windows---but rather represents a persistent behavioral regime that an agent enters and may not exit without intervention.

% Conclusion: Structural stagnation detection in LLM coding agents (EMNLP 2026 ARR)
\section{Conclusion}
\label{sec:conclusion}

We presented a systematic empirical study of progress stagnation detection in LLM coding agents, comparing structural features, neural embedding probes, and LLM-as-judge approaches against silver labels generated via weak supervision.
Three findings emerge.

First, stagnation signals are fundamentally structural.
Thirty hand-crafted features achieve 0.9951 in-domain and 0.967 cross-agent macro-F1, decisively outperforming a GRU probe (+8.96\,pp in-domain) and an LLM judge (+33.3\,pp)---all without GPU and in under 5\,ms per window.
This result holds across three embedding encoders (Qwen3, BGE-M3, E5-large), each yielding probe F1 above 0.90, confirming that the structural advantage is independent of encoder choice.
The practical implication is immediate: real-time agent monitoring need not rely on expensive representation learning or LLM inference when lightweight structural features transfer across agent architectures with minimal degradation.

Second, labeling functions exhibit systematic but agent-specific temporal dynamics.
Command repetition leads stagnation onset by 1.87 steps on SWE-Agent but reverses to a lagging role on OpenHands (+3.32 steps), where its 92.3\% firing rate and 71\% false positive rate corrupt silver labels---removing it improves fine-tuned probe F1 by 17.6\,pp.
This finding has methodological significance for weak supervision on sequential data: labeling functions validated on one domain can become adversarial on another, necessitating per-agent validation and the circular evaluation methodology we develop to surface such pathologies.

Third, temporal sophistication in label aggregation does not improve detection.
Three temporal label models---TWV, HMM, and lag-aware HMM---all fail to surpass majority vote, with TWV actually degrading downstream performance by 2.57\,pp.
This negative result constrains future research: in the low-conflict regime of 3 binary LFs (95.1\% agreement at conf${\geq}$2), temporal alignment introduces more noise than signal.

These results suggest several directions for future work.
Expanding the labeling function set beyond three functions could create the inter-LF conflict necessary for temporal aggregation to add value.
Extending evaluation to non-coding agent tasks (web browsing, data analysis, multi-agent collaboration) would test whether structural dominance generalizes beyond software engineering.
Most critically, evaluation against human-annotated ground truth---for which we have prepared a 650-window gold set with a validated annotation pipeline---will determine whether structural features detect \emph{real} stagnation or merely reconstruct labeling function outputs.

Existing approaches address aspects of this problem but fall short in three ways.
First, \emph{repetition detectors} such as cycle detection \citep{george2025cycledetection} and SpecRA \citep{pipis2025reasoningloop} identify structural repetition---exact or near-exact loops in action sequences---but by design miss semantically diverse stagnation where the agent varies its surface behavior while remaining functionally stuck.
Second, \emph{step-level scoring} via process reward models \citep{xi2025agentprm} evaluates individual actions in isolation, discarding the window-level temporal dynamics that distinguish transient setbacks from sustained stagnation---a distinction that requires reasoning over sequences of consecutive actions \citep{chen2025monitoring}.
A sequence of failed commands followed by a strategy switch, for instance, carries different diagnostic information than the same commands evaluated independently.
Third, \emph{LLM self-evaluation} \citep{shinn2023reflexion} is both expensive and fundamentally limited by the stuck model's own judgment; our LLM-as-judge baseline achieves only 0.6625 macro-F1 at \$11.66 per test set, well below lightweight feature-based alternatives.
More fundamentally, none of these approaches asks the prior question: \emph{what signals actually carry stagnation information?}
No systematic study has investigated whether detecting subtle agent failure requires sophisticated semantic understanding or whether simpler structural patterns suffice.

We address this question through a systematic empirical study (Figure~\ref{fig:pipeline}).
Using a weak supervision framework \citep{ratner2016dataprogramming,ratner2017snorkel}, we construct silver-labeled datasets from over 205K windows spanning SWE-Agent (54,809 windows, 28.5\% stagnation) and OpenHands (150,652 windows, 6.6\% stagnation).
Three labeling functions provide complementary noisy votes: command repetition ($\lambda_1$) targets repetitive behavior, file diff delta ($\lambda_2$) targets output productivity, and outcome backpropagation ($\lambda_3$) propagates task-level outcomes backward through the trajectory.

Our window-level formulation ($k{=}5$ consecutive actions, stride 1) captures short-range temporal patterns---such as repeated failures followed by strategy changes---that step-level approaches cannot express, while providing the granularity to pinpoint \emph{when} stagnation begins and ends within a trajectory, enabling targeted interventions.

Prior approaches to monitoring agent behavior address aspects of this problem but none systematically investigate what information is needed for detection.
\emph{Repetition detectors} identify exact or near-exact loops in action sequences, catching the simplest failure mode but missing semantically diverse stagnation where the agent varies its surface behavior while remaining functionally stuck.
\emph{Process reward models} \citep{xi2025agentprm} assign quality scores to individual actions, enabling search-time guidance, but step-level granularity cannot capture temporal patterns that distinguish transient setbacks from sustained stagnation---a distinction that requires reasoning over windows of consecutive actions \citep{chen2025monitoring}.
\emph{Self-reflection} frameworks \citep{shinn2023reflexion,yao2023tot,zhou2024lats} rely on the agent itself to diagnose and recover from failures, but when the agent is genuinely stuck, self-diagnosis amounts to querying the failing model about its own failure---a circularity that limits reliability.
More fundamentally, all three lines of work prescribe detection \emph{methods} without first asking what kinds of signals actually carry stagnation information: does detecting subtle agent failure require sophisticated semantic understanding, or do simpler structural patterns suffice?

We present an empirical analysis that addresses this gap.
Using a weak supervision framework \citep{ratner2016dataprogramming,ratner2017snorkel}, we construct silver-labeled datasets from trajectories of two architecturally distinct agents: SWE-Agent \citep{yang2024sweagent} on SWE-bench \citep{jimenez2024swebench} (54,809 windows) and OpenHands \citep{wang2025openhands} (150,652 windows).
Three labeling functions (LFs)---targeting command repetition, file modification patterns, and task outcome---provide noisy votes that are aggregated via majority vote into window-level binary labels.
Against these silver labels, we systematically compare three detection paradigms: hand-crafted structural features, neural embedding probes, and LLM-as-judge evaluation.

Our central finding is that \textbf{stagnation signals are fundamentally structural, not semantic}.
Thirty hand-crafted features capturing command repetition rates, file operation counts, and edit distances achieve 0.9951 macro-F1 in-domain and 0.967 on zero-shot cross-agent transfer, exceeding the LLM judge by 33.3 percentage points (pp).
A GRU-based neural probe \citep{cho2014gru} over sentence embeddings reaches 0.906 in-domain but collapses to 0.528 on zero-shot transfer and recovers only to 0.751 after full fine-tuning on the target agent.
The structural advantage is encoder-agnostic: swapping the probe's embedding backbone across three encoders (Qwen3-0.6B, BGE-M3, E5-large-v2) yields probe F1 consistently above 0.90 \citep{zhang2025qwen3embedding,chen2024bgem3,wang2024e5}, confirming that the temporal architecture rather than a specific pretrained encoder drives embedding-based performance.
Critically, the gap between structural features and learned representations persists across agents with substantially different action distributions (28.5\% vs.\ 6.6\% stagnation rates), suggesting that stagnation manifests in action-level structure that generalizes without adaptation.
This challenges the prevailing intuition that detecting subtle agent failures requires complex language understanding, and suggests that lightweight structural monitoring---requiring no GPU and running in under 5\,ms per window---may be more practical than neural or LLM-based approaches for real-time agent oversight.

Beyond static detection, we analyze the temporal dynamics of the labeling functions that generate silver labels.
On SWE-Agent, command repetition ($\lambda_1$) leads stagnation onset by 1.87 steps on average, serving as an early warning signal, while outcome backpropagation ($\lambda_3$) lags by 6.70 steps (Kruskal-Wallis $H{=}274.3$, $p{<}10^{-59}$).
However, this temporal structure is agent-specific: on OpenHands, $\lambda_1$ reverses from leading to lagging ($+3.32$ steps), firing on 92.3\% of windows with a 71\% false positive rate on progress windows.
Removing $\lambda_1$ from the OpenHands labeling pipeline improves fine-tuned probe F1 by 17.6\,pp, demonstrating that labeling functions validated on one agent architecture can become adversarial on another.
This finding establishes that LF temporal roles must be re-validated per agent and motivates the circular evaluation methodology we develop to surface such pathologies (\S\ref{sec:cmd_rep_ablation}).

We further investigate whether encoding this temporal structure into label aggregation can improve over simple majority vote.
Three temporal label models---time-varying weights (TWV), Hidden Markov Models \citep{safranchik2020linkedhmm}, and lag-aware HMMs---all fail to surpass majority vote on downstream stagnation detection.
TWV achieves marginally higher self-evaluated F1 (+0.57\,pp) but degrades downstream probe performance by 2.57\,pp; the standard HMM overpredicts stagnation, dropping downstream F1 to 0.656.
This negative result demonstrates that temporal sophistication in label aggregation does not translate to better silver labels when base agreement among LFs is already high.

Our contributions are:
\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=*,itemsep=2pt]
    \item \textbf{Structural signal discovery.} We show that 30 structural features achieve near-perfect stagnation detection (0.9951 in-domain, 0.967 cross-agent macro-F1), outperforming neural probes and LLM judges by wide margins (+33.3\,pp over LLM-as-judge). To our knowledge, this is the first systematic comparison demonstrating that stagnation information resides in action-level structure rather than semantic content.
    \item \textbf{Labeling function temporal dynamics.} We reveal that LFs occupy statistically distinct temporal niches relative to stagnation onset, with agent-specific reversals that corrupt silver labels. We develop a circular evaluation methodology to identify and quantify these cross-agent pathologies.
    \item \textbf{Temporal label model negative finding.} We show that three temporal label models fail to improve over majority vote for downstream detection, despite clear temporal structure in LF firing patterns. This informs future weak supervision design for sequential agent data.
\end{enumerate}
